# Executable Action Planning

## Operational definition

An action plan specifies a recognizable behavior, an opportunity or context,
a starting condition and enough scope to identify completion. It turns an
intention into an action that can be attempted under real constraints.

## What this concept does not mean

It is not a complete wish list, a schedule with no margin or a contingency plan
for every obstacle. Specificity cannot compensate for missing time, skill,
materials, access or authority.

## Main mechanisms

Specifying the behavior and opportunity reduces ambiguity between intending and
starting. A duration or scope boundary limits planning from expanding into an
unbounded task. Feasibility checks expose conflicts before execution.

## Evidence summary

BCTTv1 defines action planning as detailed planning of behavioral performance,
including at least one contextual element. A meta-review of self-regulation
interventions found variable support for planning and related components across
behaviors and populations; the component is not uniformly effective.

## Evidence mapping

- Action planning includes detailed planning of context and behavioral performance: `src-bcttv1-2013` (`canonical_framework`).
- Self-regulation components did not show consistent effectiveness across all reviewed domains: `src-self-regulation-2020` (`systematic_review`).

## Relevant signals

A clear intention is paired with “when I can”; the task has no recognizable
first action; a calendar block conflicts with existing commitments; or planned
scope is larger than the available opportunity.

## Alternative explanations

Non-execution may reflect insufficient ability, strong aversiveness, an imposed
goal, environmental barriers or inadequate capacity. Adding detail does not
resolve those conditions.

## Information needed

The target behavior, minimum useful scope, real opportunity, fixed commitments,
materials, dependencies, travel and available margin.

## Practical implications

Use action planning when intention and control are present but execution is
underspecified. Prefer a contingency concept when a recurring obstacle, rather
than the normal opportunity, determines the response.

## Limitations

Detailed plans can fail in unpredictable routines and can themselves become
additional work. Precision should remain proportional to the decision.

## Sources

`src-bcttv1-2013`; `src-self-regulation-2020`.

# Observable Behavior

## Operational definition

An observable-behavior description replaces a global judgment about a person
with an account that another observer could recognize: the action or non-action,
its context, frequency or duration when relevant, and its near consequence. The
unit of analysis is an episode, not a personality trait.

## What this concept does not mean

It does not deny emotions, reduce a person to metrics or require exhaustive
tracking. A precise description also does not establish why the behavior
occurred or what function it served.

## Main mechanisms

Operational description makes the target and context explicit. This permits
different explanations—opportunity, skill, energy, clarity, access, safety or
priority—to remain distinguishable instead of being collapsed into a moral
label.

## Evidence summary

BCTO and BCTTv1 provide vocabularies for specifying observable, replicable
intervention content. They are descriptive frameworks. They are not causal
tests, diagnostic instruments or evidence that observing a behavior will by
itself change it.

## Evidence mapping

- BCTO defines behavior change techniques as observable, replicable intervention components: `src-bcto-2024` (`canonical_framework`).
- BCTTv1 standardizes descriptions of intervention content: `src-bcttv1-2013` (`canonical_framework`).

## Relevant signals

The available account consists mainly of labels such as lazy, weak,
undisciplined or incapable; an intention is reported without the moment of
execution; or competing explanations depend on different episodes.

## Alternative explanations

The same non-action may reflect insufficient time, knowledge, energy, access or
priority. It may also be a reasonable response to risk or changing conditions.

## Information needed

A recent episode, the intended action, what occurred instead, the context when
it changes interpretation, and the immediate consequence. Frequency is needed
only when the decision depends on a repeated pattern.

## Practical implications

Use the smallest episode description that can discriminate the relevant
alternatives. Missing records remain missing data; they are not evidence that a
failure occurred.

## Limitations

Reports may omit context or be affected by recall. Observability improves
description, not completeness, causality or clinical validity.

## Sources

`src-bcto-2024`; `src-bcttv1-2013`.

# Chosen, Internalized and Imposed Goals

## Operational definition

Goal autonomy distinguishes goals a person endorses from goals experienced
mainly as external pressure. Internalization can be partial: a required activity
may contain personally valued reasons without becoming intrinsically enjoyable.

## What this concept does not mean

It does not reduce motivation to an intrinsic-versus-extrinsic binary, imply
that obligations are unreal, or require manufacturing enthusiasm for every
goal. External consequences and duties can remain important facts.

## Main mechanisms

Perceived choice, competence and relatedness are proposed to support more
self-determined regulation. Pressure, unclear value and low perceived capacity
can produce different patterns even when outward behavior looks similar.

## Evidence summary

A meta-analysis of randomized health-behavior trials found small average effects
for self-determination-theory interventions and reported evidence consistent
with theoretically specified mediation, alongside publication and small-sample
bias. A separate review linked need-supportive intervention strategies with
autonomy support, need satisfaction and motivation; individual strategies had
limited independent associations. These aggregate findings do not establish why
one person rejects or maintains a specific goal.

## Evidence mapping

- Self-determination-theory interventions showed aggregate effects across randomized trials: `src-sdt-rct-2020` (`meta_analysis`).
- Need-supportive strategies were associated with autonomy support, need satisfaction and motivation across interventions: `src-sdt-techniques-2019` (`meta_analysis`).

## Relevant signals

The person says the goal belongs to someone else, reports pressure as the main
reason for action, no longer sees value in the objective, or wants to stop
despite an otherwise feasible plan.

## Alternative explanations

Apparent low motivation may reflect insufficient time, sleep, skill, access,
pain, unclear requirements or an unrealistic plan. Refusing one strategy does
not prove rejection of the underlying goal.

## Information needed

Who established the goal, actual consequences of refusal, personally endorsed
value, available choice, possibilities for negotiation and costs to the person
and others.

## Practical implications

Separate non-negotiable constraints from genuine choice. The relevant decision
may be to abandon the objective, change its reason or scope, or revise the plan
while preserving a personally valued outcome.

## Limitations

This framework does not adjudicate legal, employment, educational or care
obligations. Aggregate intervention effects should not be presented as a causal
explanation for an individual's motivation.

## Sources

`src-sdt-rct-2020`; `src-sdt-techniques-2019`.

# Goal Review

## Operational definition

Goal review compares the stated objective, behavior performed, progress,
current cost and changed conditions in order to choose explicitly among keeping,
replanning, rescheduling, replacing, pausing or abandoning the goal.

## What this concept does not mean

Review is not automatic reduction whenever discomfort appears, preservation of
a goal at any cost, or treating a change in plan as abandonment of the desired
outcome.

## Main mechanisms

Separating outcome, controllable behavior, deadline, measurement and conditions
locates the mismatch. A person can execute the planned behavior without seeing
the expected progress, or make progress at a cost that changes the decision.

## Evidence summary

BCTTv1 distinguishes review of behavioral goals from review of outcome goals.
A meta-analysis by Epton and colleagues found a small positive average effect
of goal setting across behaviors, with meaningful heterogeneity and moderators.
This supports calibrated review, not a universal prescription.

## Evidence mapping

- BCTTv1 distinguishes review of behavioral and outcome goals in light of performance: `src-bcttv1-2013` (`canonical_framework`).
- Goal setting had a small positive average effect, with heterogeneity and moderators: `src-goal-setting-2017` (`meta_analysis`).

## Relevant signals

Deadlines are repeatedly moved without new information; execution is adequate
but progress is not; progress requires disproportionate cost; the goal was
externally imposed; or work, health, care duties or resources changed.

## Alternative explanations

Low apparent progress may result from a poor measure, an incompatible plan, a
short observation window, third-party dependencies or a change in priority.

## Information needed

The current objective, controllable behavior, planned versus performed action,
progress measure, cost, current importance, changed constraints and the
appropriate decision horizon.

## Practical implications

Classify the mismatch before changing the goal. Record which element changed
and what observation would justify the next review.

## Limitations

Average effects do not determine the best adjustment for one person. Values,
resources and obligations can justify decisions that do not maximize measured
performance.

## Sources

`src-bcttv1-2013`; `src-goal-setting-2017`.

# Habit Formation and Automaticity

## Operational definition

Habit formation is the gradual increase in the automaticity of a response
through repetition in contexts that provide recurring cues. Repetition can
produce a functional routine before the response feels automatic.

## What this concept does not mean

There is no universal 21-day or 66-day deadline. Habit is not synonymous with
discipline, perfect frequency, an activity placed on a calendar or every complex
routine performed regularly.

## Main mechanisms

Repeated pairing of a discriminable context with a sufficiently stable response
can reduce reliance on deliberate remembering. Simpler responses and recurring
opportunities are easier to repeat consistently than complex, variable tasks.

## Evidence summary

Lally and colleagues observed asymptotic automaticity curves and substantial
variation across 96 participants. A 2024 systematic review reported medians
around two months in a small evidence base, larger means and wide individual
ranges; many studies had high risk of bias. Context stability predicted
automaticity and repetition in two longitudinal datasets, but does not guarantee
maintenance.

## Evidence mapping

- Automaticity increased asymptotically and varied across people and behaviors: `src-habit-lally-2010` (`observational_study`).
- Formation time was widely variable in a limited, heterogeneous evidence base: `src-habit-review-2024` (`systematic_review`).
- More stable contexts predicted automaticity and repetition across one manipulated and one observational longitudinal dataset: `src-context-stability-2022` (`mixed_experimental_and_observational_longitudinal_studies`).

## Relevant signals

The action still depends on deliberate reminders, occurs in substantially
different contexts, or is too complex to function as one repeatable response.

## Alternative explanations

Forgetting may indicate an inadequate reminder rather than absent learning. Low
repetition may reflect few opportunities. A complex activity can continue to
require planning even after months of successful performance.

## Information needed

The specific response, candidate cue, actual opportunity and frequency,
complexity, weeks observed and a measure that distinguishes frequency from
subjective automaticity.

## Practical implications

Stabilizing a cue or simplifying the response may be useful when opportunities
recur. Automaticity is not required for a routine to be successful.

## Limitations

Much of the evidence relies on self-report and a limited set of health
behaviors. Findings should not be used to alter prescribed treatment or promise
a formation deadline.

## Sources

`src-habit-lally-2010`; `src-habit-review-2024`; `src-context-stability-2022`.

# Implementation Intentions

## Operational definition

An implementation intention links a discriminable situation to an available
response: if situation Y occurs, then action X will follow. It can support
starting, protecting or resuming action when a recurring obstacle appears.

## What this concept does not mean

It is not an ordinary schedule, positive thinking or an exhaustive list of
exceptions. It presupposes an endorsed goal and a response that is feasible in
the specified situation.

## Main mechanisms

The conditional link makes a relevant cue easier to recognize and preselects a
response before the obstacle occurs. This addresses execution without assuming
that strengthening intention alone will produce equivalent behavioral change.

## Evidence summary

Gollwitzer and Sheeran synthesized 94 tests and reported a positive average
effect of implementation intentions on goal attainment. Webb and Sheeran found
that experimentally changed intentions produced smaller changes in behavior,
supporting a distinction between wanting and executing. Effects vary by goal,
context and implementation quality.

## Evidence mapping

- If-then plans specifying when, where or how to act showed a positive aggregate effect on goal attainment: `src-ii-2006` (`meta_analysis`).
- Changes in intention were not fully translated into behavioral changes: `src-intention-behavior-2006` (`meta_analysis`).

## Relevant signals

The same recognizable event repeatedly precedes failure to start, interruption
or failure to resume, such as a delayed meeting, a specific distraction or a
return from travel.

## Alternative explanations

A rare, vague or uncontrollable obstacle may require capacity reserve,
negotiation or revision of the goal rather than a conditional response.

## Information needed

The endorsed goal, observable trigger, trigger frequency, control over the
response, response cost and any conflict with safety or fixed obligations.

## Practical implications

Prefer one high-value contingency over many hypothetical rules. Evaluate the
plan only after the trigger actually occurs; absence of the trigger is not
failure.

## Limitations

Aggregate effects do not guarantee individual benefit. Rigid contingencies can
be ineffective when opportunities and constraints change continuously.

## Sources

`src-ii-2006`; `src-intention-behavior-2006`.

# Physical Activity Consistency Without Individual Prescription

## Operational definition

Physical-activity consistency is repeated participation compatible with a
person's context and stated capacity. Population guidelines describe volume,
intensity and strengthening targets; they do not prescribe an individualized
starting load or progression.

## What this concept does not mean

Consistency does not require daily training, compensating for missed sessions
or continuing through pain. A population target such as 150 minutes is not a
mandatory starting point for every individual.

## Main mechanisms

Distributing feasible opportunities can support repeated participation while
preserving recovery. Population guidance provides a reference for overall
health behavior, not an algorithm for exercise programming.

## Evidence summary

WHO provides physical-activity and sedentary-behavior recommendations by age
group and emphasizes that some activity is better than none. CDC presents the
general adult reference of at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity activity
per week plus strengthening, together with cautions for specific conditions and
vigorous activity after inactivity.

## Evidence mapping

- WHO provides population recommendations for frequency, intensity and duration by age group: `src-who-pa-2020` (`institutional_guideline`).
- CDC presents adult weekly guidance and circumstances requiring professional input: `src-cdc-pa-adults` (`institutional_guideline`).

## Relevant signals

The user asks how to organize an already chosen activity, treats the weekly
reference as an all-or-nothing threshold, or proposes compensating for a missed
session by abruptly increasing volume.

## Alternative explanations

Low frequency may reflect travel, cost, care duties, preference, weather,
access or recovery. It does not establish low motivation.

## Information needed

The intended activity, current experience, available time, environment,
equipment and any known professional guidance. Clinical or critical information
is evaluated outside RAG by the Security Gate.

## Practical implications

Use guidelines as context while organizing feasible opportunities. Do not infer
individual readiness, prescribe load or technique, or define clinical
progression from completion data.

## Limitations

Population guidelines do not assess individual risk or replace qualified
exercise, rehabilitation or medical professionals.

## Sources

`src-who-pa-2020`; `src-cdc-pa-adults`.

# Functional Pattern of Procrastination

## Operational definition

Procrastination is voluntary delay despite expecting the delay to make the
outcome worse. A functional pattern describes the antecedent, alternative
action, immediate payoff and later cost before selecting an explanation.

## What this concept does not mean

Not every delay is procrastination. Missing time, information, access, ability,
decision authority or safety can make postponement reasonable or unavoidable.
The concept is not a personality label or clinical diagnosis.

## Main mechanisms

Task aversiveness, delayed rewards, low expectancy and access to more immediate
rewards can shift behavior away from an intended task. These are candidate
mechanisms; an episode-level description is needed to distinguish them from
practical constraints.

## Evidence summary

Steel's meta-analysis reported associations between procrastination and factors
including task aversiveness, reward delay, self-efficacy and impulsiveness. A
systematic review of psychological treatments found a small, heterogeneous
overall benefit across few trials. Neither synthesis identifies one universal
cause or intervention.

## Evidence mapping

- Task aversiveness, delay, self-efficacy and impulsiveness showed relevant aggregate associations: `src-procrastination-steel-2007` (`meta_analysis`).
- Psychological treatments showed a small heterogeneous benefit in a limited trial base: `src-procrastination-treatment-2018` (`systematic_review`).

## Relevant signals

The person performs peripheral preparation, switches to a more immediately
rewarding activity or waits for deadline pressure while still intending to do
the task.

## Alternative explanations

Strategic delay, a competing priority, incomplete instructions, exhaustion,
pain, an imposed goal or dependency on another person can produce similar
outward delay.

## Information needed

The chosen task, deadline, a recent episode, the alternative action, its
immediate consequence, expected later cost, available skill and resources.

## Practical implications

Match any strategy to the best-supported episode mechanism and identify an
observation that would contradict that explanation. Avoid applying a generic
anti-procrastination list.

## Limitations

Correlates are not individual causes. Persistent or disabling distress is
outside the scope of a routine-coaching explanation.

## Sources

`src-procrastination-steel-2007`; `src-procrastination-treatment-2018`.

# Retrieval Practice with Feedback

## Operational definition

Retrieval practice requires attempting to produce an answer from memory before
consulting the solution, followed by feedback or correction. The target is
retention and later use, not familiarity while looking at the material.

## What this concept does not mean

It is not merely rereading a question and answer, copying notes or taking a
high-stakes test. Repeated retrieval without corrective feedback can preserve
errors, and retrieval cannot replace initial comprehension.

## Main mechanisms

Effortful access strengthens later accessibility and reveals what cannot yet be
produced. Feedback corrects errors and distinguishes a retrieval problem from a
gap in prior understanding.

## Evidence summary

Dunlosky and colleagues rated practice testing as a high-utility learning
technique across conditions. A later classroom meta-analysis found a positive
average effect of retrieval practice, with variation by design, feedback,
material and educational context.

## Evidence mapping

- A broad evidence review rated practice testing as high utility across learning conditions: `src-learning-dunlosky-2013` (`systematic_review`).
- Classroom retrieval practice showed a positive aggregate effect with moderators and heterogeneity: `src-retrieval-meta-2021` (`meta_analysis`).

## Relevant signals

Study consists mainly of rereading or highlighting; material feels familiar but
cannot be produced without cues; or errors remain uncorrected after practice.

## Alternative explanations

Poor retrieval may reflect inadequate initial comprehension, ambiguous prompts,
missing prerequisite knowledge or a mismatch between practice and the required
application format.

## Information needed

The learning objective, material, prior understanding, expected response format,
availability and timing of correct feedback, delay until use and recurring
errors.

## Practical implications

Select prompts that require the form of knowledge needed later. Attempt an
answer before checking, correct it promptly and revisit errors rather than
counting exposure alone.

## Limitations

Effect size varies across learners, materials and settings. Retrieval practice
is not a complete curriculum and does not guarantee transfer to a substantially
different task.

## Sources

`src-learning-dunlosky-2013`; `src-retrieval-meta-2021`.

# Decision-Oriented Self-Monitoring

## Operational definition

Self-monitoring is recording a defined behavior or outcome to support a later
decision. A usable record specifies the variable, collection frequency,
observation period and the decision that the information may change.

## What this concept does not mean

It is not continuous surveillance, a score of personal worth or evidence that
an unrecorded event failed to occur. More variables and longer collection do not
automatically improve inference.

## Main mechanisms

Consistent observation can make discrepancies, context and change visible.
Defining the decision first limits collection burden and reduces the temptation
to interpret every fluctuation after the fact.

## Evidence summary

BCTTv1 defines self-monitoring of behavior and outcomes as separate techniques.
A meta-review of self-regulation interventions found variable effectiveness
across domains and components. Monitoring is therefore a way to obtain decision
data, not a guarantee of behavior change.

## Evidence mapping

- BCTTv1 distinguishes self-monitoring of behavior from self-monitoring of outcomes: `src-bcttv1-2013` (`canonical_framework`).
- Self-regulation components showed variable effectiveness across reviewed behaviors and populations: `src-self-regulation-2020` (`systematic_review`).

## Relevant signals

A decision depends on a pattern that is not yet observable; conclusions are
being drawn from incomplete coverage; or collection burden exceeds the value of
the possible decision.

## Alternative explanations

A change in the record may reflect missing entries, changed opportunities,
measurement drift or ordinary fluctuation rather than a behavioral change.

## Information needed

The decision question, observable variable, collection method, expected
coverage, burden, privacy implications, observation window and handling of
missing data.

## Practical implications

Collect the minimum variable for the shortest window that can distinguish the
relevant alternatives. Report coverage and missingness with the result.

## Limitations

Self-report and automated logs can both be incomplete. Observational patterns
do not establish causality, and intrusive collection can create privacy or
behavioral costs.

## Sources

`src-bcttv1-2013`; `src-self-regulation-2020`.

# Sleep Duration as Population Guidance

## Operational definition

Sleep duration is time actually slept over a 24-hour period. Population
recommendations provide reference ranges by age; individual need and impact also
depend on health, regularity, quality and sleep opportunity.

## What this concept does not mean

A population range is not an individual prescription or a diagnosis based on
one night. Time in bed is not necessarily time asleep, and duration alone does
not establish sleep quality.

## Main mechanisms

Regular sleep opportunity supports multiple health and functioning outcomes.
Comparing a sustained pattern with an age-appropriate reference can identify
when routine optimization should give way to a different assessment, but it
cannot identify a cause.

## Evidence summary

The American Academy of Sleep Medicine and Sleep Research Society recommend
that healthy adults sleep seven or more hours regularly to promote optimal
health. The National Sleep Foundation provides age-specific ranges based on a
multidisciplinary consensus process. Neither source supports routinely reducing
sleep to increase productivity.

## Evidence mapping

- AASM/SRS consensus recommends seven or more hours of regular sleep for healthy adults: `src-sleep-aasm-2015` (`institutional_guideline`).
- A multidisciplinary panel established recommended ranges by age group: `src-sleep-nsf-2015` (`institutional_guideline`).

## Relevant signals

Habitual sleep is substantially below the population reference, daytime
sleepiness affects functioning, or duration appears adequate while impairment
persists.

## Alternative explanations

A short measurement may be an isolated event or inaccurate estimate. Tiredness
has causes other than sleep duration, and adequate duration does not exclude
fragmented or poor-quality sleep.

## Information needed

Age, typical duration and window, duration of the pattern, daytime impact, shift
work, fragmentation and known health or medication context. Critical risk is
handled by the Security Gate before retrieval.

## Practical implications

Use the range only as a population reference. Routine planning may preserve
sleep opportunity, but causal explanation, diagnosis and treatment remain
outside this concept.

## Limitations

Consensus ranges do not measure individual need. Shift work, symptoms,
conditions and medication can require professional assessment.

## Sources

`src-sleep-aasm-2015`; `src-sleep-nsf-2015`.

# Spaced Practice

## Operational definition

Spaced practice distributes contact with and retrieval of material across more
than one session separated in time. The interval allows some forgetting while
retaining a realistic chance of successful reconstruction and correction.

## What this concept does not mean

It is not postponing first contact, applying a universal interval formula or
splitting the same total time without later retrieval. A schedule alone does not
show that learning was retained.

## Main mechanisms

Returning after a delay requires reconstruction rather than continuous
familiarity. Performance after different intervals provides information for
adjusting subsequent spacing by item difficulty and the required retention
horizon.

## Evidence summary

Dunlosky and colleagues rated distributed practice as high utility. A 2024
systematic review in health-professions education generally supported spaced
learning while reporting heterogeneous designs and outcomes. The optimal
interval depends on material, learner and how long knowledge must be retained.

## Evidence mapping

- A broad evidence review rated distributed practice as high utility: `src-learning-dunlosky-2013` (`systematic_review`).
- A recent health-professions review generally supported spaced learning but found heterogeneous implementation and outcomes: `src-spacing-review-2024` (`systematic_review`).

## Relevant signals

Most study is concentrated immediately before use; initial performance is good
but later recall is poor; or a large volume is reviewed once without later
retrieval.

## Alternative explanations

Low later performance may reflect weak initial comprehension. Spacing material
that was not understood can repeat confusion rather than resolve it.

## Information needed

The date and form of later use, material units, current understanding, available
opportunities, retrieval difficulty after intervals and total time constraints.

## Practical implications

Schedule at least two later retrieval opportunities when the horizon permits.
Shorten intervals for items that cannot yet be reconstructed and lengthen them
when retrieval is consistently successful.

## Limitations

The recent review is concentrated in health-professions education. No single
interval is optimal across materials, learners or retention horizons.

## Sources

`src-learning-dunlosky-2013`; `src-spacing-review-2024`.

# Environmental Cues and Behavioral Friction

## Operational definition

An environmental cue is a recurring feature of a situation that can make a response more likely to be noticed or initiated. Behavioral friction is the observable effort, delay, number of steps or access barrier between an opportunity and that response.

## What this concept does not mean

The environment does not determine behavior, and every failure to act is not a cue problem. “Friction” is not a diagnosis or a substitute for checking skill, capacity, goal endorsement and real opportunity.

## Main mechanisms

Stable contexts can repeatedly expose the same response opportunity. A context change can remove a previously useful cue. Materials that are unavailable, extra setup steps or a competing default can increase response cost even when intention remains unchanged.

## Evidence summary

A natural experiment involving university transfers found that established behaviors were more likely to persist when relevant context features remained stable. In one longitudinal study, students were assigned to stable or variable habit-building contexts; a second longitudinal app dataset measured naturally occurring context stability. Both showed greater stability associated with more repetition and automaticity. These studies support context-sensitive hypotheses, not a universal claim that rearranging an environment changes behavior.

## Evidence mapping

- Changed circumstances disrupted some context-cued behaviors: `src-habit-discontinuity-2005` (`longitudinal_natural_experiment`).
- Context stability was examined in one manipulated and one observational longitudinal dataset: `src-context-stability-2022` (`mixed_experimental_and_observational_longitudinal_studies`).

## Relevant signals

The same missing item, setup step, location change or competing default precedes nonperformance across more than one genuine opportunity.

## Alternative explanations

There may have been no time, the first action may be unclear, the task may be aversive, or the goal may no longer be chosen.

## Information needed

The latest opportunity, location, preceding event, materials, number of setup steps, competing action and whether the response occurs in a different context.

## Practical implications

Change one observed barrier or make one relevant cue more discriminable, then compare comparable opportunities. Preserve access and privacy; do not make the environment coercive.

## Limitations

The evidence is largely observational and behavior-specific. A cue that helps one response may distract from another, and complex activities continue to require planning.

## Sources

`src-habit-discontinuity-2005`; `src-context-stability-2022`.

# Graded Task Progression

## Operational definition

Graded task progression starts with a version that is within demonstrated capacity and increases difficulty in planned steps toward the target behavior. A grade can change duration, frequency, complexity, resistance or required independence.

## What this concept does not mean

It is not indefinite reduction, permission to ignore a chosen goal, or a universal rule to make every task tiny. It does not prescribe exercise load, rehabilitation or treatment progression.

## Main mechanisms

A feasible grade creates an opportunity to practice the relevant response and collect feedback. Predetermined progression conditions reduce the chance that a temporary surge in confidence becomes an untested increase across several dimensions.

## Evidence summary

The BCT Taxonomy defines graded tasks as setting easy-to-perform tasks and increasing difficulty until the target behavior is performed. A systematic review and meta-analysis of physical-activity interventions for adults with overweight or obesity found graded tasks among positive moderators in some analyses. This is domain-limited, component-level evidence and does not establish an optimal progression rate for an individual.

## Evidence mapping

- Graded tasks are a distinct, operationally defined behavior-change technique: `src-bcttv1-2013` (`consensus_taxonomy`).
- Graded tasks moderated effects in a specific physical-activity intervention literature: `src-graded-pa-2021` (`systematic_review_meta_analysis`).

## Relevant signals

The current version is repeatedly not completed despite real opportunities, or the user wants to increase several load dimensions after only brief success.

## Alternative explanations

The task may lack instructions, materials or endorsement. Noncompletion may reflect scheduling rather than task difficulty.

## Information needed

Current dose, recent completion and cost, target dose, safety constraints, dimension to change and a review interval.

## Practical implications

Keep the target visible, choose one feasible grade and define what evidence would justify changing one dimension. For physical or clinical activity, defer to applicable professional guidance.

## Limitations

Technique labels do not prove isolated efficacy. Evidence varies by behavior and population, and easier tasks can be irrelevant if they do not preserve the target response.

## Sources

`src-bcttv1-2013`; `src-graded-pa-2021`.

# Lapses, Streaks and Behavioral Recovery

## Operational definition

A lapse is a missed intended response during one or more genuine opportunities. Recovery is the return to a feasible next response after checking whether the opportunity, context, capacity or goal changed.

## What this concept does not mean

A lapse is not proof that a habit has disappeared, that prior repetitions were wasted or that the person lacks discipline. A streak is a count of consecutive recorded performances, not a direct measure of automaticity, quality or long-term maintenance.

## Main mechanisms

Habit learning accumulates through repeated cue-response experience and follows variable trajectories. A missed opportunity changes the record but does not logically erase prior learning. A longer interruption may expose changed contexts or capacity and therefore requires reassessment rather than automatic compensation.

## Evidence summary

In Lally and colleagues' observational model, missing one opportunity did not materially affect the automaticity trajectory, although this result came from a small sample and should not be generalized to every interruption. A later systematic review found wide variation in formation time and methods. Together, the evidence supports avoiding all-or-nothing conclusions, not promising that any lapse is harmless.

## Evidence mapping

- A single missed opportunity did not materially affect modelled automaticity in the observed sample: `src-habit-lally-2010` (`observational_study`).
- Habit trajectories and estimates varied substantially across a limited literature: `src-habit-review-2024` (`systematic_review`).

## Relevant signals

Several planned opportunities were missed, the user treats a broken streak as total loss, or proposes a sharp workload increase to “catch up.”

## Alternative explanations

The schedule, health, resources, cue or chosen goal may have changed. The record may also be incomplete.

## Information needed

Which opportunities were real, what changed before the first miss, current capacity, the next available opportunity and whether the goal remains endorsed.

## Practical implications

Resume at the next feasible grade, redistribute only when constraints allow, and review the cause if misses cluster. Judge recovery by renewed behavior and cost, not by restoring a streak.

## Limitations

Direct evidence about everyday “streaks” is sparse. This concept should not be used for substance-use relapse, eating disorders, medication adherence or other clinical conditions.

## Sources

`src-habit-lally-2010`; `src-habit-review-2024`.

# Task Aversiveness and Delay

## Operational definition

Task aversiveness is the anticipated or experienced unpleasantness of engaging in a particular task. It can involve boredom, frustration, resentment, stress or other negative experience and may differ across stages of the same project.

## What this concept does not mean

It is not laziness, a stable personality label or proof that the task should be abandoned. A task can be important and chosen while still feeling aversive.

## Main mechanisms

Avoiding or postponing an aversive task can provide immediate relief. That short-term consequence can compete with a delayed task outcome, especially when the first productive action is costly or benefits remain distant.

## Evidence summary

Blunt and Pychyl found that boredom, frustration and resentment clustered with task aversiveness across project stages in an undergraduate sample, with other components varying by stage. Steel's meta-analytic review identified task aversiveness as a strong and consistent correlate of procrastination. These findings support a task-specific hypothesis but do not establish aversiveness as the cause of an individual's delay.

## Evidence mapping

- Aversiveness included recurring and stage-specific dimensions: `src-task-aversiveness-2000` (`cross_sectional_primary_study`).
- Task aversiveness was consistently associated with procrastination across the reviewed literature: `src-procrastination-steel-2007` (`meta_analytic_review`).

## Relevant signals

The user knows the first action and has opportunity and capacity, yet describes dread, boredom, frustration or relief immediately after switching away.

## Alternative explanations

The action may be ambiguous, a prerequisite may be missing, the goal may be imposed, or capacity may be insufficient.

## Information needed

The latest delayed action, anticipated unpleasant aspect, substitute action, immediate consequence, goal endorsement and whether aversiveness changes after beginning.

## Practical implications

Match the response to the observed component: clarify a frustrating dependency, bound an unpleasant interval, change a recurring environmental barrier, or reconsider an unendorsed goal. Test one change.

## Limitations

Much of the evidence is correlational and student-heavy. Reducing discomfort does not guarantee completion, and persistent severe distress requires a different assessment.

## Sources

`src-task-aversiveness-2000`; `src-procrastination-steel-2007`.

# Temporal Discounting in Procrastination

## Operational definition

Temporal discounting is the reduction in subjective value assigned to an outcome as its delay increases. In procrastination, immediate relief or an available reward may outweigh a valued but distant benefit at the decision point.

## What this concept does not mean

It does not mean that every delay is impulsive, irrational or caused by one brain system. Choosing an immediate need can be reasonable when constraints or uncertainty change.

## Main mechanisms

The cost of beginning is experienced now, while completion benefits and many consequences arrive later. As a deadline approaches, the delayed consequence becomes more immediate, which can change the relative value of acting.

## Evidence summary

Steel's meta-analytic review found that task delay and impulsiveness were consistent predictors within a temporal motivation account. A 2024 study measured work progress over a real semester task and found a positive correlation between delay discounting and procrastination using the full progress trajectory, but not using completion day or self-report alone. This measurement sensitivity and correlational design require caution.

## Evidence mapping

- Delay-related predictors were consistent with temporal motivation theory: `src-procrastination-steel-2007` (`meta_analytic_review`).
- Discount rate correlated with a trajectory-based measure of real-world procrastination: `src-temporal-discounting-2024` (`correlational_primary_study`).

## Relevant signals

Work accelerates only near deadlines, an immediately rewarding substitute repeatedly wins, or the user explicitly describes present relief as stronger than a distant outcome.

## Alternative explanations

The deadline may be artificial, the first action unclear, the task aversive, or the outcome insufficiently valued.

## Information needed

Timing of costs and benefits, actual deadline, substitute reward, progress trajectory, first action and whether delay occurs without distant outcomes.

## Practical implications

Make progress and consequences nearer and observable, reduce delay to useful feedback, or precommit a concrete opportunity. Do not assume reward engineering is necessary before the pattern is observed.

## Limitations

One recent real-world study cannot establish individual causation. Discounting measures and procrastination measures are not interchangeable.

## Sources

`src-temporal-discounting-2024`; `src-procrastination-steel-2007`.

# Perfectionistic Concerns and Evaluative Avoidance

## Operational definition

Evaluative avoidance is postponement or withholding that occurs when producing or exposing work creates an anticipated evaluative threat. The relevant perfectionistic dimension is usually concern about mistakes, discrepancy or external evaluation, not high standards by themselves.

## What this concept does not mean

Perfectionism is not a unitary explanation for procrastination. Careful work, ambitious standards and revision are not avoidance when they remain proportionate and lead to delivery.

## Main mechanisms

Delaying exposure can temporarily reduce the possibility of receiving evidence that performance falls short. Repeated checking or revision can also function as a safer substitute for submitting, testing or requesting feedback.

## Evidence summary

A 2017 meta-analysis found a positive association between procrastination and perfectionistic concerns, but a negative association with perfectionistic strivings. Steel's earlier review found only weak relationships for some fear-of-failure and socially prescribed perfectionism constructs. The combined evidence argues for assessing the specific concern and behavior rather than labeling the user a perfectionist.

## Evidence mapping

- Perfectionistic concerns and strivings showed different average relationships with procrastination: `src-procrastination-perfectionism-2017` (`meta_analysis`).
- Fear-of-failure constructs were not uniformly strong predictors: `src-procrastination-steel-2007` (`meta_analytic_review`).

## Relevant signals

Work is repeatedly revised but not exposed, a safe preparation activity replaces an evaluable output, or the user names anticipated judgment or mistakes at the decision point.

## Alternative explanations

The quality criterion may genuinely be unclear, the output may carry material risk, prerequisite skill may be missing, or more time may be justified.

## Information needed

The required standard, current draft state, who evaluates it, consequences of error, last delivery attempt and what would count as sufficient evidence for completion.

## Practical implications

Define a fit-for-purpose completion criterion and the smallest real exposure that can produce useful feedback. Preserve necessary quality and safety checks.

## Limitations

Most evidence is correlational. Fear, standards and delay can influence one another, and this concept is not a clinical assessment of anxiety or personality.

## Sources

`src-procrastination-perfectionism-2017`; `src-procrastination-steel-2007`.

# Behavior Goals and Outcome Goals

## Operational definition

An outcome goal specifies a result, such as a score or completed project. A behavior goal specifies an observable action the person can perform. A process goal is useful here only when it names behavior rather than an internal slogan.

## What this concept does not mean

Outcome goals are not inherently bad, and behavior goals do not guarantee outcomes. Translating a result into action should not erase why the result matters.

## Main mechanisms

Outcome goals orient direction and evaluation. Behavior goals identify controllable responses that can be scheduled, observed and revised. Keeping both levels prevents a desired result from being mistaken for an executable plan.

## Evidence summary

The BCT Taxonomy distinguishes goal setting for behavior from goal setting for an outcome, supporting precise intervention description rather than superiority of either type. A meta-analysis of randomized behavior-change studies found a small positive unique average effect of goal setting with substantial moderator dependence. Evidence therefore supports using the distinction to improve decision clarity, not promising that one goal format will produce success.

## Evidence mapping

- Behavior and outcome goal setting have distinct operational definitions: `src-bcttv1-2013` (`consensus_taxonomy`).
- Goal setting produced a small average effect across heterogeneous behavior-change trials: `src-goal-setting-2017` (`systematic_review_meta_analysis`).

## Relevant signals

The user names only a desired result, tracks an outcome with delayed or external determinants, or cannot say which repeated action would make progress more likely.

## Alternative explanations

The next action may already be known but blocked by resources, capacity, conflict or aversiveness.

## Information needed

Desired result, controllable actions, external dependencies, measurement delay and the shortest useful review period.

## Practical implications

Retain the outcome as direction, add one observable behavior that is plausibly related, and monitor both without claiming individual causality.

## Limitations

Terminology varies across fields. The evidence does not support converting every meaningful aspiration into a single metric or ignoring outcome quality.

## Sources

`src-bcttv1-2013`; `src-goal-setting-2017`.

# Goal Specificity

## Operational definition

Goal specificity is the degree to which a target identifies a discriminable result or performance level. An action plan separately states the behavior, context and timing used to pursue that target.

## What this concept does not mean

Specificity is not the same as difficulty, personal importance, measurability of every private experience or a complete execution plan. A precise target can still be impossible, imposed or strategically wrong.

## Main mechanisms

A specific target can direct attention, effort and evaluation toward a defined discrepancy. It also permits feedback to be interpreted against a reference. Planning then translates that reference into situated action.

## Evidence summary

Locke and Latham's review of goal-setting research describes specificity and difficulty as core goal properties whose effects depend on commitment, feedback, ability and task complexity. The BCT Taxonomy distinguishes goal setting from action planning and behavioral observation. Together, these sources support keeping the target and the execution plan conceptually distinct; they do not establish one universally effective specification format.

## Evidence mapping

- Specific goals can direct performance through attention, effort, persistence and strategy under important moderators: `src-goal-theory-2002` (`narrative_theoretical_review`).
- Goal setting and action planning are separately defined intervention components: `src-bcttv1-2013` (`consensus_taxonomy`).

## Relevant signals

Terms such as “improve,” “be consistent” or “get organized” have no defined target, observable indicator or boundary.

## Alternative explanations

The target may be clear while the first action, opportunity, resources or priority remain unclear.

## Information needed

Desired change, target level or boundary, observable indicator, timeframe appropriate to the behavior and who controls the outcome.

## Practical implications

Specify the target only as far as needed for a real decision, then create an action plan. For exploratory work, a bounded learning goal may be more appropriate than a premature performance target.

## Limitations

Classic evidence is concentrated in performance settings and cannot justify a universal “SMART” formula. Excess specificity can narrow attention or imply false precision.

## Sources

`src-goal-theory-2002`; `src-bcttv1-2013`.

# Goal Difficulty and Feasibility

## Operational definition

Goal difficulty is the level of performance or change required relative to current capability and conditions. Feasibility asks whether the target can plausibly be pursued with available time, skill, resources, feedback and dependencies.

## What this concept does not mean

More difficult is not always better, and feasibility is not an invitation to eliminate challenge. A missed target alone does not reveal whether difficulty, execution, measurement or context was responsible.

## Main mechanisms

Challenging specific goals can focus effort and persistence when commitment, ability, task knowledge and feedback are adequate. As complexity or uncertainty rises, learning, strategy development and staged progression may matter more than a fixed performance demand.

## Evidence summary

Locke and Latham's review describes a positive difficulty-performance relation under important moderators and boundary conditions. Epton and colleagues found that difficult goals moderated stronger average effects in randomized behavior-change studies, but the overall goal-setting effect was small and studies were heterogeneous. Neither source supplies an individually optimal difficulty level.

## Evidence mapping

- Ability, commitment, feedback and complexity moderate goal effects: `src-goal-theory-2002` (`narrative_theoretical_review`).
- Difficult goals were associated with larger average effects in one behavior-change meta-analysis: `src-goal-setting-2017` (`systematic_review_meta_analysis`).

## Relevant signals

The required pace exceeds demonstrated performance, depends on unavailable resources, combines several untested increases or leaves no allowance for known constraints.

## Alternative explanations

The goal may be feasible but vague, poorly scheduled, externally imposed or competing with another goal.

## Information needed

Baseline performance, target and deadline, skill, resources, dependencies, recent cost, uncertainty and acceptable minimum.

## Practical implications

Identify which constraint makes the current target implausible. Adjust one of scope, pace, deadline, support or progression, then define a review point using observed performance and cost.

## Limitations

Much classic evidence concerns assigned performance tasks. This concept does not set clinical, educational or exercise prescriptions and should preserve domain-specific safety rules.

## Sources

`src-goal-theory-2002`; `src-goal-setting-2017`.

# Conflict and Facilitation Between Goals

## Operational definition

Goal conflict exists when pursuing one valued goal hinders another through incompatible strategies or competition for finite resources. Goal facilitation exists when pursuit of one goal supports another through shared means or outcomes.

## What this concept does not mean

Having several goals is not automatically conflict. Conflict and facilitation are not necessarily opposite ends of one scale: the same pair can share resources in one context and compete in another.

## Main mechanisms

Resource conflict consumes the same time, money, attention or recovery capacity. Inherent conflict uses strategies whose successful execution undermines each other. Facilitation can arise from shared actions, environments or intermediate outcomes.

## Evidence summary

A meta-analysis of 54 samples found goal conflict associated on average with lower positive outcomes and greater distress, with results varying by measurement and sample. Three multimethod studies by Riediger and Freund supported distinguishing interference from facilitation and linked them differently to well-being and persistent pursuit. These associations do not establish that conflict caused an individual's distress or nonperformance.

## Evidence mapping

- Goal conflict showed average associations with well-being and distress: `src-goal-conflict-meta-2017` (`meta_analysis`).
- Interference and facilitation behaved as distinct goal relations: `src-goal-interference-2004` (`multimethod_primary_studies`).

## Relevant signals

Two actions require the same limited period or resource, success in one undermines the other, or switching between goals repeatedly prevents meaningful progress.

## Alternative explanations

The goals may coexist but be overplanned, vague or individually infeasible. Apparent conflict may be a scheduling problem.

## Information needed

Each valued goal, required behaviors, shared constraints, incompatible strategies, deadlines, minimum viable progress and possible shared actions.

## Practical implications

Classify the conflict before prioritizing. Options include redesigning shared means, separating contexts, sequencing goals, reducing one target or deliberately deprioritizing one after checking autonomy and consequences.

## Limitations

Measures of goal conflict vary and much evidence is correlational. The concept should not turn every difficult value choice into a technical optimization problem.

## Sources

`src-goal-conflict-meta-2017`; `src-goal-interference-2004`.

# Estimating Task Duration

## Operational definition

A task-duration estimate is a forecast from a defined start condition to a defined completion condition. Its quality depends on task boundaries, comparable observations, dependencies and uncertainty, not only confidence.

## What this concept does not mean

Every underestimate is not a planning fallacy, and a single multiplier is not a universal correction. Delays can reflect changed scope, interruptions, missing dependencies or a different definition of done.

## Main mechanisms

People can focus on a coherent future scenario while underusing the distribution of relevant past completion times. Multifaceted tasks also hide components and transitions that are absent from a single global estimate.

## Evidence summary

Buehler, Griffin and Ross found optimistic predictions for personal completion times across several studies and observed reliance on future scenarios over relevant past experience. Kruger and Evans found that prompting people to unpack multifaceted tasks produced longer estimates and reduced bias in some experiments, with stronger effects for more complex tasks. Replication and task differences preclude treating decomposition as a guaranteed correction.

## Evidence mapping

- Personal completion forecasts were often optimistic and insufficiently anchored in prior experience: `src-planning-fallacy-1994` (`experimental_primary_studies`).
- Unpacking improved estimates for some multifaceted tasks and conditions: `src-planning-unpacking-2004` (`experimental_primary_studies`).

## Relevant signals

Comparable tasks repeatedly exceed estimates, planning includes only productive steps, or the completion boundary changes during execution.

## Alternative explanations

The task may be genuinely novel, scope may be unstable, records may omit interruptions, or external dependencies may dominate duration.

## Information needed

Start and done definitions, component steps, transition and setup time, comparable actuals, dependencies, interruptions and confidence range.

## Practical implications

Use comparable recorded durations when available, unpack only meaningful components, include dependencies and state a range. Update the estimate after execution rather than moralizing the error.

## Limitations

The foundational experiments used bounded tasks and student samples. Forecasting large projects or safety-critical work requires domain-specific methods.

## Sources

`src-planning-fallacy-1994`; `src-planning-unpacking-2004`.

# Variability in Motivational State

## Operational definition

A motivational state is a time-varying willingness to initiate or sustain goal-directed effort. It is distinct from whether the goal is endorsed and from a stable description of the person.

## What this concept does not mean

Motivation is not irrelevant, and low motivation does not always call for acting anyway. A sharp or persistent change can reflect sleep, health, mood, overload, context or loss of goal endorsement.

## Main mechanisms

Momentary willingness changes the subjective balance between effort and reward. A prior cue-linked plan can reduce the need to make the entire decision again at the action point, but only after a goal is chosen.

## Evidence summary

An intensive longitudinal study sampled adults repeatedly over 15 days and found substantial state variation; momentary motivation prospectively predicted reward sensitivity and effort-based choices. The design does not show that state motivation caused every subsequent choice or that plans eliminate state effects. A meta-analysis of implementation intentions found average benefits for goal achievement while retaining dependence on prior intention, context and plan quality.

## Evidence mapping

- Motivation varied within people and related prospectively to effort-based choice: `src-motivation-fluctuation-2025` (`intensive_longitudinal_study`).
- If-then planning supported goal striving on average: `src-ii-2006` (`meta_analysis`).

## Relevant signals

The user postpones until a preferred feeling arrives, action varies with daily willingness despite recurring opportunities, or a brief surge drives an oversized plan.

## Alternative explanations

The goal may be imposed, the task aversive, capacity insufficient, or the opportunity poorly specified.

## Information needed

Whether the goal remains chosen, recent motivation and action pattern, sleep or capacity changes, actual opportunity, minimum useful action and safety signals.

## Practical implications

Treat motivation as information and a variable condition. If the goal remains endorsed and capacity is adequate, plan a feasible action anchored to an opportunity and review what happened across several occasions.

## Limitations

The longitudinal study measured effort-based decisions, not every routine behavior. This concept is not an assessment of depression, apathy or another health condition.

## Sources

`src-motivation-fluctuation-2025`; `src-ii-2006`.

# Behavioral Feedback for Adjustment

## Operational definition

Behavioral feedback is information about observed action or outcome interpreted against a defined reference and used to decide whether to maintain, investigate or adjust a plan.

## What this concept does not mean

A score is not automatically useful feedback. Feedback is not praise, blame, surveillance or a causal explanation. More frequent reporting is not always better.

## Main mechanisms

Monitoring creates a record; feedback connects that record to a goal or expectation. The discrepancy, stability and cost of performance can inform whether the next decision is to preserve the current mechanism, change one variable or gather more information.

## Evidence summary

A meta-analysis of 138 experimental studies found that interventions increasing progress monitoring improved goal attainment on average, with larger effects in some reporting and recording conditions. A meta-review of health behavior found personalized feedback among sometimes successful self-regulation components, but no component worked consistently across behaviors and populations. Feedback should therefore remain specific and actionable without being treated as universally effective.

## Evidence mapping

- Increasing progress monitoring promoted goal attainment on average: `src-progress-monitoring-2016` (`meta_analysis_of_experiments`).
- Feedback and other self-regulation components had heterogeneous effects: `src-self-regulation-2020` (`systematic_meta_review`).

## Relevant signals

Records exist but are used only for judgment, stable progress triggers needless escalation, or repeated misses do not lead to a defined review.

## Alternative explanations

The measure may be invalid, opportunities incomparable, the reference inappropriate or the observation window too short.

## Information needed

Behavior and outcome measures, reference, observation window, comparable opportunities, performance cost and the decision the data can change.

## Practical implications

State the observation separately from interpretation. Maintain a working plan when progress and cost are stable; otherwise adjust one plausible variable for a defined test period.

## Limitations

Monitoring interventions often contain multiple components and may change behavior through reporting or accountability. Feedback can demotivate or mislead when measures are poor.

## Sources

`src-progress-monitoring-2016`; `src-self-regulation-2020`.

# Interleaved Practice

## Operational definition

Interleaved practice mixes examples or problem types from different categories so the learner must discriminate which category, concept or procedure applies. Blocked practice groups one type together.

## What this concept does not mean

Interleaving is not random multitasking, rapid switching between unrelated subjects or a universal replacement for initial instruction and blocked familiarization.

## Main mechanisms

Adjacent contrast can highlight differences between categories, and mixed problems require selecting a method rather than repeating a recently demonstrated procedure. Interleaving may also introduce spacing, so the two mechanisms can be difficult to separate.

## Evidence summary

A multilevel meta-analysis of 59 studies found a moderate overall interleaving effect but strong moderation by material: benefits were larger for some visual categories and mathematics, ambiguous for expository texts and reversed for word materials. Dunlosky and colleagues likewise treated interleaved practice as promising but less broadly established than practice testing and distributed practice.

## Evidence mapping

- The average interleaving effect depended substantially on material and similarity structure: `src-interleaving-meta-2019` (`meta_analysis`).
- Interleaving had narrower evidence than retrieval and distributed practice in a broad learning review: `src-learning-dunlosky-2013` (`evidence_review`).

## Relevant signals

The assessment requires distinguishing similar categories or selecting among procedures, while blocked practice produces success only when the method is obvious from order.

## Alternative explanations

Errors may reflect missing foundational knowledge, insufficient retrieval, inadequate feedback or practice that is too difficult.

## Information needed

Learning objective, category similarity, current mastery, test format, feedback availability and whether learners must select a method.

## Practical implications

Use a small set of related categories, require an explicit choice, provide corrective feedback and compare delayed discrimination with blocked practice. Retain blocks for initial acquisition when needed.

## Limitations

Effects do not generalize across all materials, and laboratory schedules differ from complete courses. Subjective difficulty is not proof of learning.

## Sources

`src-interleaving-meta-2019`; `src-learning-dunlosky-2013`.

# Fluency and Miscalibrated Learning Judgments

## Operational definition

Processing fluency is the subjective ease of perceiving or processing material. A miscalibrated learning judgment occurs when that ease or familiarity is used as evidence of later retrieval or transfer beyond what performance supports.

## What this concept does not mean

Easy processing is not always misleading, and difficult study is not automatically effective. “Desirable difficulty” requires better later learning, not discomfort by itself.

## Main mechanisms

Recent exposure, repeated reading and blocked examples can make material feel accessible while the answer remains present. That cue differs from producing the answer after a delay without support, which more closely samples later retrieval demands.

## Evidence summary

Yan and colleagues experimentally found that blocked presentation created fluent category processing and contributed to mistaken beliefs about the relative benefit of blocking versus interleaving; correcting the illusion was difficult. Dunlosky and colleagues rated practice testing and distributed practice as broadly useful, while rereading had lower and less durable utility. These findings support performance checks but not a claim that every feeling of familiarity is false.

## Evidence mapping

- Fluency and prior beliefs contributed to misjudging blocked and interleaved learning: `src-metacognitive-illusion-2016` (`experimental_primary_studies`).
- Practice testing had stronger general utility than rereading in a broad review: `src-learning-dunlosky-2013` (`evidence_review`).

## Relevant signals

Recognition is high with notes open but unaided recall fails later, repeated reading drives confidence without testing, or a blocked set feels mastered only while the procedure is signaled.

## Alternative explanations

Poor later performance may reflect inadequate spacing, unclear questions, insufficient instruction or test anxiety rather than judgment error.

## Information needed

Target performance, study method, delay, cues available during study and test, prediction of performance and actual unaided result.

## Practical implications

Sample learning with brief delayed retrieval or application under target-like cues, then compare confidence with performance. Use the discrepancy to choose restudy, feedback or further retrieval.

## Limitations

Metacognitive accuracy varies by task and learner. One check is noisy, and high-stakes assessment requires valid, representative questions.

## Sources

`src-metacognitive-illusion-2016`; `src-learning-dunlosky-2013`.

# Sleep Timing Regularity

## Operational definition

Sleep regularity is the day-to-day consistency of sleep onset and wake timing. It is a dimension of sleep health distinct from duration, quality and sleep-disorder symptoms.

## What this concept does not mean

Regular timing does not compensate for insufficient sleep, and one variable weekend is not a diagnosis. Regularity guidance should not override shift-work realities, caregiving, treatment plans or an acute need for recovery sleep.

## Main mechanisms

Stable sleep and wake timing can support alignment between behavior and circadian timing. Variability may reflect or contribute to misalignment, but observational associations can also arise from work, illness, stress and social conditions.

## Evidence summary

A National Sleep Foundation panel used a systematic review and formal consensus process and concluded that consistency of sleep onset and offset is important for health, safety and performance. The panel also noted that catch-up sleep may help when weekday sleep is insufficient. A 2020 systematic review of 41 studies found later timing and greater variability generally associated with adverse outcomes, but evidence quality ranged from very low to moderate and thresholds could not be identified.

## Evidence mapping

- A formal expert panel endorsed sleep-timing consistency while preserving a catch-up-sleep qualification: `src-sleep-regularity-consensus-2023` (`formal_consensus_with_systematic_review`).
- Sleep variability was generally associated with adverse adult health outcomes without clear thresholds: `src-sleep-consistency-review-2020` (`systematic_review`).

## Relevant signals

Bed or wake times vary widely across comparable days, weekday and weekend timing repeatedly diverge, or tiredness follows schedule shifts despite adequate recorded duration.

## Alternative explanations

Insufficient duration, insomnia symptoms, shift work, substances, caregiving, illness or measurement error may better explain the pattern.

## Information needed

Sleep and wake times across at least a week, duration, day types, naps, work constraints, symptoms and applicable security-gate signals.

## Practical implications

If safe and feasible, test a consistent wake or sleep opportunity across comparable days while protecting adequate duration. Escalate health concerns rather than coaching around them.

## Limitations

Much evidence is observational, metrics differ and no universal variability threshold is established. This document is not medical advice.

## Sources

`src-sleep-regularity-consensus-2023`; `src-sleep-consistency-review-2020`.
